clue.text: Guardian errs? Blow not half bad for latter-day 22!

indicators.note: bad here means poorly formed, so the letters before it are to be rearranged
only half of the word blow is used, its first two letters

explanation.surface: A newspaper's mistakes are a blow, half-blamed on its modern editor.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram takes GUARDIAN, ERRS and BL (half of 'Blow') together. 22 is the answer to 22-down, the Guardian's great editor C. P. Scott.
explanation.definitionFit: Alan Rusbridger edited the Guardian from 1995 to 2015, a modern successor to C. P. Scott in that chair.

clue.text: Members dropping off when the cost is high?

definitions.text: Members dropping off when the cost is high?

parts.words: Members dropping off when the cost is high?
parts.note: limbs (members) lost as the price of something very expensive, the idiom for an exorbitant cost

explanation.surface: Club members leave when the subscription rises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Members' suggests a club, but it means limbs: an arm and a leg are what you pay, idiomatically, for something very expensive.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a very high price as if paid in body parts, matching a steep cost.

clue.text: Gazelle off the ground, we hear

indicators.note: we hear signals that the word is judged by its sound, not its spelling

parts.note: aerial means in the air, off the ground

explanation.surface: A gazelle leaps clear of the earth, so people say.
explanation.walkthrough: The grid prints ARIAL (a typeface); the gazelle is spelt ARIEL, the word that sounds like 'aerial', and the fourth letter is unchecked.
explanation.definitionFit: An ariel is a species of Middle Eastern gazelle, a sense found in larger dictionaries.

clue.text: What could be aide's approximation

parts.note: aide is a jumbled form of the word idea, so it is what a 'rough' version of idea could produce

explanation.surface: An assistant's estimate.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: read the answer as wordplay, 'rough' an anagram signal on IDEA, and it yields AIDE; 'What could be' joins.
explanation.definitionFit: A rough idea is a loose estimate or approximation of something.

clue.text: Is priest turning up in satin? No money for another fabric

indicators.note: in places the reversed letters inside the trimmed word
no here means the money is taken away from the word satin

parts.note: tin is slang for money

indicators.note: in a down clue turning up means reading the letters from the bottom upwards

parts.note: Eli is the priest in the Old Testament book of Samuel

explanation.surface: A priest appears in satin, but with no money he moves on to a cheaper cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No money' removes TIN from SATIN to leave SA; 'turning up' reverses IS + ELI to ILESI, which goes 'in' SA.
explanation.definitionFit: Silesia is a twilled cotton lining fabric, named after the region, so it is another material besides satin.

clue.text: Dismiss with regret ruffian becoming audible

indicators.note: becoming audible means the words are to be taken as heard spoken

parts.note: to rue is to regret; a lout is a rough, uncouth man

explanation.surface: A remorseful thug gets thrown out once he starts shouting.
explanation.definitionFit: To rule out a possibility is to dismiss it from consideration.

clue.text: Campaign rubbish left to be disposed of

indicators.note: to be disposed of says the letter for left is thrown out of the word

parts.note: drivel is rubbish, nonsense

explanation.surface: A campaign to get rubbish taken away.
explanation.definitionFit: A drive is an organised campaign, such as a recruitment or fundraising drive.

clue.text: I'm obsessed with myself — come again when things have changed

indicators.note: when things have changed tells us the letters of the previous words must be altered in order

explanation.surface: A narcissist tells someone to return once circumstances are different.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is spoken by the answer: someone saying they are obsessed with themselves describes themself.
explanation.definitionFit: An egomaniac is a person obsessively preoccupied with themself, so the line is their self-description.

clue.text: Last word from 3 going to university

parts.note: 3 points to 3-down, a rough idea: the word idea roughly rearranged, giving these letters

explanation.surface: A rough idea's final remark on leaving for college.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference is wordplay: 3-down is ROUGH IDEA, read as IDEA jumbled, here as ADIE.
explanation.definitionFit: Adieu is a farewell, the last thing said on parting.

clue.text: Sweet supply brought back with tablet about to be swallowed

indicators.note: to be swallowed puts one part inside another
brought back reverses the word for supply

parts.note: a pool is a shared supply, as of labour or cars

indicators.note: about here means turned round, reversing the tablet

parts.note: a pill is a tablet

explanation.surface: Confectionery stock is returned with a pill about to be gulped.
explanation.walkthrough: Two separate reversals are signalled, 'brought back' for the supply and 'about' for the tablet, before one swallows the other.
explanation.definitionFit: A lollipop is a hard sweet on a stick.

clue.text: See 16
Maiden given a pound, so must become an economist

parts.note: M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over
L is the abbreviation for pound, from Latin libra
thus means so, therefore

explanation.surface: A young woman handed a pound must turn into a money expert.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Malthus was the English economist famous for his theory of population growth.

clue.text: Outside work Irish girl's involved in

indicators.note: involved in says the girl is wrapped inside the other letters

parts.note: op is short for opus, a work
Ena is a girl's name; the 's here means 'is'

explanation.surface: A girl from Ireland is taking part in an outdoor job.
explanation.definitionFit: Open-air means happening outdoors, outside rather than in a building.

clue.text: Observed as a respectable youth in the fifties?

definitions.meaning: observed means noticed or remarked upon

definitions.text: a respectable youth in the fifties?
definitions.meaning: a decent young man of the 1950s was no Teddy boy

explanation.walkthrough: Teddy boys (Teds) were 1950s British youths in Edwardian-style clothes, seen as troublemakers; a respectable lad was 'no Ted'.
explanation.definitionFit: Noted means observed or remarked, as in noting a detail.

clue.text: Mum comes upon fox in part of wood? That could be a fluke

indicators.note: in puts the mother and fox inside the wood's part

parts.note: a tree is one part of a wood

indicators.note: in a down clue comes upon means sits above, so one piece is placed before the other

parts.note: ma is an informal word for mum
tod is a dialect word for a fox

explanation.surface: A mother stumbles on a fox among the trees, which might just be luck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fluke' looks like luck, but it means the parasitic flatworm.
explanation.definitionFit: Trematodes are parasitic flatworms commonly called flukes.

clue.text: Grotesque streak in fold of rock

parts.note: antic as an adjective means grotesque or bizarre
a line is a streak or stripe

explanation.surface: An odd vein runs through a folded rock layer.
explanation.definitionFit: In geology an anticline is an arch-shaped fold in rock strata.

clue.text: 22 frames fab career dictum — seen around here

definitions.text: 22 frames fab career dictum — seen around here

indicators.note: around signals all the letters being moved about into a new order

parts.note: 22 refers to 22-down, the Guardian editor C. P. Scott

explanation.surface: The great editor frames a fine saying from his career, one seen in this paper.
explanation.walkthrough: Scott's 1921 maxim is spread over three lights; 'here' is the Guardian itself, which runs a section named after its opening.
explanation.definitionFit: C. P. Scott wrote this maxim in a 1921 essay; it remains the Guardian's founding editorial principle.

clue.text: See 16
Endorse silly symbol for charity

indicators.note: silly suggests the letters of the previous word are to be jumbled

explanation.surface: Backing a daft emblem for a good cause.
explanation.walkthrough: Red Nose Day is a British Comic Relief fundraiser for which people wear red plastic noses.
explanation.definitionFit: The red nose is the emblem of Comic Relief, a British charity telethon.

clue.text: Put down from job, being deficient in performance

definitions.meaning: removed from office, as a ruler or official
lacking a pose, a pose being a performance or act

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the word: DE- means lacking, and a pose is a put-on performance.
explanation.definitionFit: To be deposed is to be removed from a position of power, ousted from one's post.

clue.text: Lay off historian appearing in Asian territory

indicators.note: off says the word lay is taken away from the historian's name

parts.note: Thomas Babington Macaulay was the Victorian historian of England

explanation.surface: A historian is laid off and turns up in Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lay off' reads as a phrase, but 'off' acts on 'Lay', removing it from MACAULAY.
explanation.definitionFit: Macau is a former Portuguese territory on the south China coast, now a special administrative region.

clue.text: 1 across or 22 admitting mistake went by

indicators.note: admitting means letting in, so the mistake goes inside

parts.note: both 1 across and 22-down were Guardian editors, and ED is short for editor
a lapse is a slip or mistake

explanation.surface: An editor owns up to an error as time passes.
explanation.definitionFit: Elapsed means passed, as time goes by.

clue.text: Papers finally put to bed on time? He'd have made sure of that

definitions.text: He'd have made sure of that

indicators.note: finally takes the last letter of the word papers

parts.note: a cot is a small bed

explanation.surface: Newspapers go to press punctually, as a famous editor would insist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put to bed' is press jargon for sending a paper to print; here 'put to' is a link and 'on' joins T after COT.
explanation.definitionFit: C. P. Scott, the Guardian's long-serving editor, would have ensured papers went to press on time.

clue.text: Somehow remove hunter of fox, letting animal escape

parts.note: John Peel was the famous Cumbrian huntsman of the song
of is taken as written

indicators.note: letting along with escape tells us the animal leaves the word fox
escape along with letting removes the animal from fox

parts.note: an ox is an animal

explanation.surface: Somehow a fox-hunter's quarry gets away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'D'ye ken John Peel' is an English hunting song celebrating a Cumbrian huntsman; the first clue word adds only colour to the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To peel off something is to remove it, such as a layer or label.

clue.text: Weight with which man outside club keeps extreme characters away

indicators.note: keeps extreme characters away removes the first and last letters of the word

parts.note: a bouncer guards the door of a nightclub

explanation.surface: A doorman at a club keeps the wild types out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extreme characters' seems to mean troublemakers but means the first and last letters, B and R.
explanation.definitionFit: An ounce is a unit of weight, a sixteenth of a pound.

clue.text: Wake up without energy after party and look blue

indicators.note: after places the shortened rouse behind party and look

parts.note: a do is a party
lo means look, as in lo and behold

indicators.note: without means the energy is left out

parts.note: to rouse is to wake up
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Getting up drained after a party and looking glum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look blue' wants to be the definition, but 'look' is LO and only 'blue' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Dolorous means sorrowful, which is what feeling blue is.

clue.text: Cold eccentric goes round without one item of clothing

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside places the first part around the next
goes round turns the cold eccentric back to front

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps
a nut is an eccentric person
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A chilly oddball walks about without a single garment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like lacking, but it means outside: C + NUT reversed is TUNC, which goes round I.
explanation.definitionFit: A tunic is a loose garment, a simple item of clothing.

clue.text: Splashing suds thereafter and cleaning items

indicators.note: splashing suggests the letters of suds and thereafter are thrown about

explanation.surface: Soapy water splashes about and then come the dusters.
explanation.definitionFit: Feather dusters are household cleaning tools made of feathers on a handle.
